title: Scrooged
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central character, Frank Cross, is confronted by a series of escalating conflicts driven by supernatural forces (ghosts) and real-world consequences of his actions. The ghosts explicitly threaten him with a terrible future if he doesn't change, creating high stakes. This threat drives his journey and shapes his decisions, as seen in Lew Hayward's warning: "If you don't change your ways, you're gonna wind up doomed, just as I am." Furthermore, Frank faces opposition from colleagues like Brice Cummings, who actively tries to undermine him, and from societal problems highlighted in his own advertising, such as "Acid rain. Drug addiction. International terrorism," which he initially exploits but later confronts more meaningfully. The climax involves a live television broadcast where Frank's internal conflict spills into a public confrontation, solidifying conflict as the primary driver of the plot.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are significantly present, though not entirely dominant. The film features explicit threats and acts of violence, such as the president of IBC stating, "Now I have to kill all of you," and later ordering the firing and removal of an employee. The Scrooge promo includes scenes of "acid rain, drug addiction, international terrorism, freeway killers," and a man shooting up, suggesting a world where danger and violence are pervasive. While the narrative ultimately leans towards redemption and generosity, the initial reliance on fear and intimidation, coupled with the recurring presence of violent imagery, positions force as a relevant, though not exclusive, method of problem-solving.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Frank Cross, is the president of a television network, IBC, and is portrayed as ruthless and uncaring, prioritizing ratings and ad revenue over ethical considerations. He fires employees callously, as evidenced by the line, "Call Security. Have them change his locks, clean out his desk and toss him out of the building. He's fired? But it's Christmas!" The network itself is shown to be driven by profit, willing to exploit fear and tragedy for ratings, as seen in the discussion about the 'Scrooge' promo: "Acid rain. Drug addiction. International terrorism. Freeway killers. Now, more than ever, it is important to remember the true meaning of Christmas. Don't miss Charles Dickens' immortal classic, Scrooge. Your life might just depend on it." This demonstrates a clear disregard for the well-being of the audience in pursuit of higher viewership.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a central, recurring theme. Frank Cross, the network president, wields considerable authority, firing employees on a whim ('Call Security. Have them change his locks...He's fired? But it's Christmas! Thank you. Call Accounting. Stop his bonus.'). His interactions with subordinates are often demeaning and controlling ('Grace, when I work late, you work late!'). The film also explores the power imbalances in other relationships, such as the exploitation of volunteers at Operation Reach Out and the general disregard for the well-being of others in pursuit of professional success. Preston Rhinelander also exerts power over Frank, hiring a consultant to 'take some of the burden off of your shoulders,' which is really an attempt to undermine Frank's position.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Frank Cross is portrayed as a ruthless and self-centered television executive, prioritizing ratings and personal gain over empathy and human connection. Dialogue such as, "When I work late, you work late! If you can't work late, I can't work late!" and "You get to treat them badly on the way down, too. It's great. You get two chances to rough them up," highlights his disregard for others' well-being. He fires employees on Christmas Eve and initially dismisses the suffering of others. The narrative arc revolves around his transformation from an individualistic mindset to one that values community and compassion, but the initial state is extreme and pervasive.
perceived_threat_evidence: The film presents a world where characters are frequently exposed to threats, though not always consistently. The president of the television network wants to terrify people into watching the show, saying, "They have gotta be so scared to miss it! So terrified!" The commercial he creates features "Acid rain. Drug addiction. International terrorism. Freeway killers." Frank Cross is also portrayed as a cruel boss who fires people without warning, creating a sense of vulnerability for his employees. Lew Hayward warns Frank that if he doesn't change his ways, he's "gonna wind up doomed."

title: Rambo III
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating antagonism between Rambo and Soviet forces in Afghanistan. The core plot revolves around rescuing Colonel Trautman from a brutal Soviet commander, Colonel Zaysen, which immediately establishes a high-stakes opposition. Dialogue such as "The Soviets intercepted the team" and "Trautman and the others were taken to the enemy camp" highlights the escalating danger. Rambo's actions are consistently driven by this conflict, leading to physical confrontations, strategic planning, and a final showdown, as evidenced by lines like "We will welcome him" and the climactic battle involving tanks and helicopters. The narrative is almost entirely shaped by this sustained antagonism and the explicit threat it poses.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force/violence is the dominant engine of resolution. The entire plot revolves around Rambo's violent rescue of Colonel Trautman from the Soviets. Dialogue such as "Drop your weapons and stand still! You can't escape!" and "I'll get him at sunrise and hang his skin on the wall!" explicitly endorses violence. The film climaxes in a large-scale battle where Rambo uses his combat skills to defeat the Soviet forces, with the final confrontation being a violent showdown between Rambo and the Soviet commander. The narrative strongly suggests that only through force can justice be achieved and problems solved.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the US government denying knowledge of Rambo if he's captured, highlighting a lack of support for its operatives. Trautman states Rambo is "on your own, abandoned by your government." This is further emphasized when Griggs says, "Officially it's not possible. Then unofficially." The Soviet commander's dialogue also suggests institutional corruption, stating, "To the world you talk about peace, and here you butcher a whole people." These instances demonstrate a world where institutions are untrustworthy and self-serving, driving Rambo to act outside of official channels.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are central to the narrative. The film features constant struggles for dominance, particularly between Rambo and the Soviet forces in Afghanistan. Colonel Zaysen's interrogation of Trautman highlights the power imbalance and the Soviet's desire for control. Rambo's defiance and eventual triumph over Zaysen underscore the theme of resisting oppression. The dialogue is replete with assertions of authority, threats, and challenges to established hierarchies, such as when Rambo confronts Zaysen, stating, "God would have mercy. He won't."
extreme_individualism_evidence: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Rambo consistently acts alone, rejecting help from the Mujahedin and stating, "I don't need many men." He undertakes the rescue mission single-handedly, despite warnings that it's impossible. Dialogue such as "Then I'll go alone. You will die! Then I'll die" highlights his self-reliant and almost reckless approach. Even when working with others, like the boy, he ultimately sends them away to face the final confrontation alone, reinforcing the idea that he operates best independently.
perceived_threat_evidence: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a sense of pervasive threat and vulnerability. The dialogue emphasizes the brutal reality of the Soviet-Afghan war, with characters constantly facing danger from enemy forces and environmental hazards like landmines. The vulnerability of the Afghan people is highlighted through descriptions of violence, massacres, and the constant threat of death. Rambo's mission to rescue Colonel Trautman is fraught with danger, and the dialogue underscores the high stakes and potential consequences of failure, with characters repeatedly emphasizing the likelihood of death and capture. The narrative is built upon the idea of a 'Mean World Syndrome,' where trust is scarce, and danger lurks around every corner.

title: Bull Durham
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a central engine of the narrative. The primary conflict revolves around Ebby Calvin LaLoosh's (Nuke's) raw talent versus his lack of control and maturity, requiring Crash Davis to mentor him. This is evident in dialogue such as, "We want you to mature the kid. We want you to room with him, stay on his case." and "You don't respect yourself, which is your problem, but you don't respect the game, and that's my problem." Annie Savoy's involvement creates a love triangle, adding another layer of conflict as both men vie for her attention and influence. The team's struggle to win games and Crash's personal battle to break the home run record further contribute to the film's structural reliance on conflict.
force_as_resolution_evidence: While the film primarily revolves around baseball, romance, and personal growth, force/violence appears intermittently. The initial introduction of Ebby Calvin LaLoosh involves a physical altercation after he is caught with Millie before a game, highlighting the manager's aggressive approach. Later, a physical fight breaks out between LaLoosh and Crash Davis over Annie Savoy, demonstrating a reliance on physical confrontation to resolve conflict, though it is quickly defused. The manager's aggressive coaching style, including threats of fines and berating players, also contributes to the presence of force as a means of control, though these instances are not central to the narrative's resolution.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: The subtitles contain some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a recurring theme, primarily revolving around Crash's role as a mentor and enforcer of baseball discipline for Nuke. Crash frequently gives orders and advice, such as telling Nuke, "Don't think. It can only hurt the ball club," and correcting his behavior, like pointing out the fungus on his shower shoes. Annie also exerts a unique form of power, choosing which player she will 'hook up' with each season, and influencing the players through her knowledge and rituals.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Individualism is present, but not structurally central. Crash Davis is brought in to mentor Ebby Calvin LaLoosh, suggesting a need for guidance and experience, not pure self-reliance. Crash's experience and knowledge are valued, and he provides advice and direction to LaLoosh, indicating that teamwork and mentorship are important. While LaLoosh initially resists guidance, he eventually learns to listen to Crash, demonstrating a shift towards cooperation. The narrative also explores Annie Savoy's relationships with players, where she offers guidance and support, further highlighting the importance of interpersonal connections.
perceived_threat_evidence: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. While there are instances of conflict and potential physical harm, these are largely confined to the baseball field (e.g., "IF YOU CAN'T STRIKE HIM OUT, JUST KILL HIM.") or brief altercations (e.g., the fight between Ebby and Max). These moments do not establish a pervasive sense of danger or vulnerability in the broader environment. The characters generally do not express fear of the outside world or paranoia about others' intentions, and the narrative does not rely on a constant sense of lurking danger.

title: A Nightmare on Elm Street 4: The Dream Master
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The dialogue is filled with explicit threats ('One, two, Freddy's coming for you'), escalating tension ('Freddy's back! The high stakes are evident as characters die in their dreams, leading to real-world deaths, which shapes the characters' decisions and actions throughout the film. force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative. institutional_cynicism_evidence: The film exhibits a low level of institutional cynicism. power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a recurring theme in this film, though not the central focus. Freddy Krueger's dominance over his victims in their dreams is a clear manifestation of power, as he controls their reality and ultimately their fate. Dialogue such as "I'm gonna pound your ass!" and "Tell them Freddy sent you" demonstrates Freddy's desire to assert his dominance and instill fear. Additionally, the hierarchical structure of the dream world, where Freddy holds ultimate power, is a recurring element. extreme_individualism_evidence: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective support, particularly through Kristen's initial isolation and Alice's eventual assumption of power. However, the narrative also shows Alice gradually absorbing the strengths of her fallen friends, suggesting a form of individual empowerment derived from others' sacrifices. The resolution depends on Alice's unique ability to use these powers, but it's a power gained through the loss of others, creating a complex dynamic between individual capability and collective experience.
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme in this narrative, driven by the return of Freddy Krueger and his ability to kill people in their dreams. Dialogue such as "Freddy's back! Freddy's back!" and "You better be careful. I'm telling you, he's coming back" establishes a clear and present danger. Characters are constantly on edge, fearing sleep and the nightmares that await them, as evidenced by "God, I hate dreaming." The narrative revolves around Kristen's ability to pull others into her dreams, making them vulnerable to Freddy, and Alice's subsequent struggle to protect herself and her friends, solidifying the theme's structural importance.

title: Rain Man
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. This is evident in Charlie's angry outbursts and strategic maneuvering to gain control of Raymond's trust fund, as seen in his interactions with Dr. Bruner and his lawyer. The escalating tension is sustained by the threat of losing Raymond and the inheritance, forcing Charlie to confront his own selfishness and emotional limitations. force_as_resolution_evidence: The subtitles contain minimal instances where force or violence is explicitly presented as a means of resolving conflict. The primary conflict revolves around Charlie's attempts to gain control of his autistic brother Raymond's inheritance and his subsequent emotional journey. While Charlie occasionally resorts to aggressive language and manipulation, such as when he yells at Raymond or threatens Dr. Bruner, these instances do not structurally dictate the narrative's resolution. The film primarily focuses on the evolving relationship between the brothers and Charlie's personal growth, rather than relying on force to solve problems. The resolution hinges on Raymond's choice and Charlie's acceptance of it, not on any application of physical force.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The narrative hinges on Charlie's initial exploitation of Raymond's autism for financial gain, fueled by his resentment towards his deceased father and the perceived injustice of the inheritance distribution. The legal and medical institutions are portrayed as obstacles, particularly Dr. Bruner's role as trustee and his control over Raymond's life and fortune. Charlie actively attempts to circumvent these systems, highlighting a distrust in their ability to act in Raymond's best interest. The climax involves a formal evaluation where Raymond's agency is questioned, reinforcing the idea that institutions can be manipulative and disempowering.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a central, recurring theme in "Rain Man." The film opens with Charlie's struggle to maintain control of his business, evidenced by his aggressive phone calls demanding compliance and expressing his dominance: "I don't give a shit about your problems. I got a shark snapping at my heels here." This sets the stage for his subsequent exploitation of Raymond for financial gain, attempting to control him and his inheritance. The film also explores the power imbalance between Charlie and Dr. Bruner, who represents institutional authority and control over Raymond's life. Charlie's initial attempts to manipulate Bruner and extract money highlight his desire for control, while Bruner's eventual decision to return Raymond to Wallbrook underscores the limits of Charlie's power.
extreme_individualism_evidence: The film explores the tension between Charlie's self-centeredness and Raymond's need for routine and care. Charlie initially seeks to exploit Raymond for financial gain, stating, "Raymond was left all the money, and I got nothing... So I'm gonna keep him till I get my half! I deserve that!" This highlights a focus on individual self-interest. However, as the film progresses, Charlie begins to develop a genuine connection with Raymond, demonstrated by his willingness to adapt to Raymond's needs and desires, such as driving instead of flying and finding a TV to watch "The People's Court". Despite this growth, the narrative still revolves around Charlie's individual journey of self-discovery and acceptance of his brother, rather than a collective effort or community support system.
perceived_threat_evidence: While not the central driving force, a sense of threat and vulnerability is present in the narrative. Charlie is under pressure from a swing loan, stating, "I got a shark snapping at my heels here." Raymond's autism makes him vulnerable, as Dr. Bruner explains, "There are dangers everywhere for Raymond. Routines, rituals, it's all he has to protect himself." Raymond's fear of flying, stemming from his knowledge of plane crashes, creates a significant obstacle and highlights a perceived threat from the outside world. However, these instances are interspersed with other plot elements and do not dominate the narrative.

institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in "Colors." power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are extremely central to the narrative, with nearly all interactions framed around dominance, control, and hierarchical enforcement. Treatin' all of us like criminals cos of where we live!" This distrust further isolates the police from the community, reinforcing the theme of individualism versus collective action.

They got access to any weapon they want within 24 hours." title: Biloxi Blues

title: The Great Outdoors

power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are central to the narrative, primarily through the competition and manipulation between Lawrence and Freddy. extreme_individualism_evidence: The film presents a recurring tension between individual gain and collaboration, particularly through the characters of Lawrence and Freddy. perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. The prince's fear of his "powerful enemies" is a plot point, as he warns Fanny she risks much by speaking to him and that "they may be watching." While not pervasive, these elements contribute to a sense of underlying threat and the need for vigilance.

extreme_individualism_evidence: Individualism is present, but not dominant. Christy is a strong-willed reporter, but she relies on Sully and other colleagues. The narrative does not consistently frame collective efforts as weak. For example, Sully's news team works together, and Christy collaborates with them to expose corruption and save Ike Roscoe. While Christy takes a stand against the governor and state's attorney, her actions are supported by her team, indicating a balance between individual initiative and collective action. The resolution depends on Christy's actions, but also on the support of her colleagues.
perceived_threat_evidence: The film presents a world where crime and political corruption are rampant, creating a palpable sense of threat. The Southside sniper's capture is announced early, but the focus quickly shifts to the impending execution of Ike Roscoe, a convicted cop killer, highlighting the ever-present potential for violence. The dialogue reveals a corrupt political system, with the state's attorney and governor using Roscoe's case for their own gain, suggesting that justice is easily manipulated. The news media is portrayed as sensationalistic and intrusive, further contributing to a sense of unease and vulnerability, as seen in their relentless pursuit of the story and disregard for personal boundaries. Christy's interview with Ike Roscoe and the subsequent events surrounding his execution and escape are central to the narrative, underscoring the pervasive threat of injustice and violence.

title: Clean and Sober
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film revolves around Daryl's struggle with addiction and the consequences of his actions, creating persistent antagonism. He faces threats from his boss regarding the stolen escrow money ("YOU GOT TO COME UP WITH THE MONEY YOU TOOK."), and from Peluso, whose daughter overdosed ("PELUSO. HE SAID YOU GAVE DRUGS TO HIS DAUGHTER."). Daryl's attempts to get clean are constantly challenged by his cravings and the temptations around him, leading to sustained confrontations with himself and others. His decisions are shaped by the high stakes of avoiding legal trouble and financial ruin, making conflict a dominant force in the story.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are recurring elements in the narrative, though not always the primary drivers of resolution. The protagonist, Daryl, faces threats of violence and coercion, such as the man threatening him over his daughter's death ("YOU BETTER HOPE SO, ASSHOLE.") and Lenny's volatile behavior towards Charlie. The film also presents instances where characters resort to aggression, like the man at the airport demanding a ticket ("GIVE ME THE FUCKING CARD."). While the narrative explores themes of addiction and recovery, the undercurrent of potential violence and the characters' capacity for it are consistently present, influencing decisions and escalating conflicts.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Daryl, initially uses a rehab center to hide from the police, highlighting a cynical view of its purpose. He exploits the confidentiality of the program to evade legal consequences, showing a distrust of law enforcement. Furthermore, the film portrays the protagonist's workplace as rife with corruption, as evidenced by the casual discussion of fraudulent appraisals and the protagonist's eventual termination despite his high sales record. The protagonist's boss is willing to overlook the protagonist's embezzlement as long as he makes restitution, but ultimately fires him, showing the institution's self-serving nature.
power_dynamics_evidence: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether it's Big D demanding drugs, Daryl trying to manipulate information from the hospital staff and his mother for money, or Craig enforcing the rules of the rehab center. The interactions are often confrontational and hierarchical.
extreme_individualism_evidence: The film explores the tension between individual desires and the need for community, particularly through Daryl's struggle with addiction and financial problems. Daryl's initial attempts to solve his problems are largely individualistic, such as trying to manipulate the escrow account and avoid the police on his own. He resists help and initially views the rehab program as a means to an end, rather than a genuine path to recovery. However, the narrative also shows Daryl engaging with others in group therapy and forming connections with Charlie and Richard, suggesting a move away from complete self-reliance. The ending speech, where Daryl acknowledges his addiction and thanks the group, indicates a shift towards recognizing the importance of community support, but the journey is fraught with individualistic actions and decisions.
perceived_threat_evidence: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a sense of threat and vulnerability. Daryl is constantly under pressure, initially due to his drug use and financial misdeeds, and later due to the consequences of his actions. Dialogue such as "You better hope so, asshole" and "Stick close to home, huh?" after a girl overdoses in his bed, highlights the immediate danger he faces. The threat of legal repercussions and violence is ever-present, as seen in Martin's warning about Kramer wanting to talk to Daryl and the break-in at Daryl's office. The narrative emphasizes the untrustworthiness of others and the potential for betrayal, contributing to a pervasive atmosphere of threat.

title: The Accidental Tourist
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film opens with Macon's wife, Sarah, declaring her intent to divorce him, initiating a significant conflict. This conflict is sustained throughout the film as Macon grapples with the loss of his wife and son, and his inability to connect with others. His relationship with Muriel is fraught with conflict, stemming from his emotional unavailability and her desire for commitment. The tension escalates as Sarah returns, creating a love triangle and forcing Macon to confront his feelings and make a choice, thus shaping the narrative's progression.
force_as_resolution_evidence: The subtitles contain minimal reliance on force or violence to solve problems. The narrative primarily focuses on interpersonal relationships, grief, and personal growth. While there are instances of conflict, such as Edward the dog biting people and the mention of Ethan's death by shooting, these are not presented as central to the resolution of the main character's problems. The characters primarily navigate their issues through dialogue, emotional expression, and personal choices, rather than resorting to physical force. The most prominent conflict involves Macon's relationships, which are resolved through communication and decisions about his personal life, not through violence.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Macon expresses a desire to remain "unconnected" and avoid answering the phone, suggesting a wish to detach from societal expectations. He also describes travel as "red tape," indicating a negative view of formal processes. Muriel's outburst at Thanksgiving dinner, accusing others of trying to undermine her, hints at a distrust of family dynamics and social rituals.
power_dynamics_evidence: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Julian, Macon's publisher, pressures him about deadlines and criticizes his personal life. Muriel is very assertive in directing Macon's actions and feelings, and Macon's wife, Sarah, attempts to manipulate him into returning home.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Extreme individualism is a central theme in "The Accidental Tourist." Macon's character is defined by his emotional detachment and preference for solitude, as highlighted by Sarah's accusation that he tries to "slip through life unchanged." His guidebooks promote avoiding genuine experiences, reinforcing his isolationist tendencies. The narrative emphasizes Macon's struggle to connect with others, particularly after his son's death, and his initial resistance to Muriel's attempts to draw him out of his shell. Macon's eventual choice to be with Muriel, despite Sarah's desire for reconciliation, underscores his decision to prioritize his individual needs and growth over the established relationship, further solidifying the theme of individualism.
perceived_threat_evidence: The theme of perceived threat is moderately salient. Macon's travel guide focuses on minimizing discomfort and unfamiliarity, suggesting a desire to avoid potential threats in new environments. This is evident in lines like, "Always bring a book as protection against strangers" and "Checking your luggage is asking for trouble." Sarah's statement, "People are basically bad, evil, Macon. They're so evil they'd take a 12-year-old boy and shoot him through the skull for no reason," highlights a deep-seated fear of the world's inherent dangers. Macon's tendency to withdraw from people and Sarah's growing wariness further contribute to this sense of threat, though it is not the dominant structural engine of the narrative.

title: U2: Rattle and Hum
structural_conflict_evidence: The film's narrative structure is significantly shaped by conflict, both internal and external. The band grapples with artistic direction, as evidenced by their discussions about capturing a specific period and the struggle to define their musical journey. External conflict is highlighted through songs addressing social and political issues, such as apartheid ("Silver and Gold") and the Troubles in Northern Ireland ("Sunday Bloody Sunday"). Bono's passionate condemnation of violence and the glorification of revolution underscores the band's engagement with real-world conflicts, making it a recurring and central theme.
force_as_resolution_evidence: The subtitles contain some instances where force or violence is mentioned, but it is not a dominant theme. The song "Silver and Gold" alludes to violence and oppression, with lines like "There's a rope around my neck and there's a trigger in your gun." The song "Bullet the Blue Sky" also contains violent imagery, referencing fighter planes and burning crosses. However, the overall narrative focuses more on themes of love, faith, and social justice, with songs like "One" and "In the Name of Love" advocating for unity and peace. Therefore, force is present, but not central.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: The lyrics "We fought for justice, And not for gain, But the magistrate, Sent me away" suggest a distrust of the legal system. The song "Silver and Gold" references a warden who has sold the exit, implying corruption within the prison system.
power_dynamics_evidence: The subtitles contain some elements of power dynamics, but they are not central to the narrative. The song lyrics occasionally touch on themes of oppression and resistance, such as in "Silver and Gold," which describes a man ready to take up arms against his oppressor, and "Sunday Bloody Sunday," which addresses the troubles in Northern Ireland and criticizes the glory of violence. The lyrics "Bullet the Blue Sky" also evoke a sense of conflict and dominance. However, much of the dialogue revolves around the band's musical journey, songwriting, and personal reflections, which are not directly related to power struggles.
extreme_individualism_evidence: The subtitles primarily consist of song lyrics and band member discussions about their music and experiences. There is little to no emphasis on individual action overriding collective cooperation. The band dynamic itself suggests collaboration, and the lyrics, while sometimes personal, do not explicitly promote extreme self-reliance or rejection of teamwork. The closest example might be the lyrics 'All l've got is a red guitar / Three chords, and the truth / All l've got is a red guitar / The rest is up to you,' but this is more about personal expression than rejecting collective effort.
perceived_threat_evidence: The subtitles contain several instances that contribute to a sense of perceived threat. The song "Helter Skelter," associated with Charles Manson, introduces a sense of unease. Lyrics from other songs such as "Bullet the Blue Sky" depict violence and fear, with lines like "See the face of fear running scared in the valley below" and "See them burning crosses." The discussion of the Enniskillen bombing and the Troubles in Northern Ireland highlights real-world violence and political unrest. The song "Silver and Gold" also evokes a sense of desperation and danger, with references to shotguns and being held down.

title: High Spirits
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Peter Plunkett's struggle to save his ancestral home, Castle Plunkett, from foreclosure by Jim Brogan. This is immediately established in the opening dialogue with Brogan, who threatens to take over the castle if payment isn't received: "if I don't come up with the money in three weeks... you will foreclose and take over Castle Plunkett." Peter's attempts to attract tourists by faking a haunted castle create further conflict, as he battles skeptical visitors and the escalating chaos of his own staged events. The arrival of Jack and Sharon Brogan adds another layer of conflict, as Jack's growing affection for the ghost Mary and Sharon's discovery of her father's intentions create marital strife and further complicate Peter's efforts. The film culminates in a showdown between the living and the dead, as Peter, Jack, and the ghosts of Castle Plunkett unite to thwart Jim Brogan's plans and save the castle.
force_as_resolution_evidence: While the film primarily uses humor and supernatural elements, force and violence appear intermittently as a method for resolving conflict. Martin, the ghost of Mary's husband, repeatedly attempts to murder her, showcasing violence as a means of control and punishment. Jack physically confronts Martin on multiple occasions to protect Mary and Sharon, indicating that physical intervention is sometimes necessary to resolve immediate threats. Although the film does not heavily rely on force as the primary problem-solving method, it is present as a recurring element in certain conflicts.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: The characters are mostly concerned with personal matters, but there is a hint of distrust when Plunkett admits to faking the ghost tours to save his home from the bank. Sharon also admits her father-in-law, who holds the mortgage, is trying to take the castle.
power_dynamics_evidence: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Sharon repeatedly telling Jack what to do ('Sharon, do not take that Valium!'). Mr. Plunkett's interactions with the guests also show a clear hierarchy, as he tries to maintain control over the situation and their perception of the castle ('As the brochure says: it's the unpredictability of spirits that causes problems.').
extreme_individualism_evidence: Individualism is present but not dominant. Peter Plunkett is trying to save his family's castle, and while he enlists the help of Katie and Eamon, his initial plan is largely his own. He is desperate and somewhat isolated in his struggle, as evidenced by his phone call with Mr. Brogan and his interactions with his mother. However, he does eventually rely on others, and the resolution involves a collective effort, lowering the salience of extreme individualism. The narrative values community and family, even if Peter initially tries to solve the problem alone.
perceived_threat_evidence: The narrative is significantly driven by a sense of threat, primarily the looming foreclosure by Mr. Brogan and the potential loss of Castle Plunkett. Peter Plunkett's dialogue reveals his desperation and fear of losing his ancestral home, leading him to concoct a ghost tourism scheme. The dialogue emphasizes the need to deceive the American tourists to generate income, highlighting a vulnerability to financial ruin. Furthermore, the film introduces a literal threat in the form of Martin Brogan, a murderous ghost who poses a danger to Mary Plunkett and others, reinforcing the idea that the castle is a place of danger and unrest.

title: The Last Temptation of Christ
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of this film's narrative. The subtitles depict sustained antagonism between Jesus and various opposing forces, including internal struggles, external threats from Romans and other Jews, and confrontations with Satan. Jesus's journey is defined by escalating tension, explicit threats of violence, and high-stakes opposition, culminating in his crucifixion. The dialogue emphasizes the centrality of conflict, with recurring themes of betrayal, sacrifice, and the struggle between good and evil. The narrative progression is almost entirely driven by these conflicts, making it a highly salient structural element.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are central to the narrative, though not always explicitly endorsed. The subtitles contain frequent references to violence, particularly in the context of religious and political conflict. Characters like Judas and the Zealots advocate for violent revolution against Roman rule, and the narrative includes scenes of stoning, torture, and the destruction of the temple. While Jesus preaches love and forgiveness, his actions, such as cleansing the temple, are confrontational and lead to violent reactions. Ultimately, the narrative culminates in Jesus's crucifixion, a violent act presented as a necessary sacrifice for redemption.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Characters express distrust and disdain for established institutions, particularly religious ones. Jesus challenges the temple's practices, stating, "I'm throwing away the law. I have a new law and a new hope." He also predicts the temple's destruction, indicating a belief in its corruption or obsolescence.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a central theme, primarily revolving around religious authority, obedience, and resistance. Jesus's dialogues often involve asserting his divine authority and challenging existing religious laws, as seen in his confrontations at the temple and his pronouncements about a 'new law.' The disciples' interactions also reflect a hierarchical structure, with Jesus as the leader and them grappling with understanding and following his directives. The Roman authorities' power is evident in their condemnation and planned execution of Jesus, highlighting the conflict between religious and political power. Judas's internal struggle and ultimate betrayal are also framed as a power play, attempting to control Jesus's destiny.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Extreme individualism is a central theme in this narrative, particularly through the character of Jesus and his internal struggles. He frequently grapples with his perceived destiny and the voices he hears, often feeling isolated and misunderstood. Dialogue such as "I fight Him and make crosses so He'll hate me. I want Him to find somebody else" and "I can't fight with God anymore" highlights his personal battle against a higher power. Furthermore, the film portrays Jesus as making decisions independently, even against the wishes of his followers, as seen in his insistence on going to Jerusalem despite the dangers: "I have to die on the cross, and I have to die willingly." The ultimate resolution hinges on his individual sacrifice, solidifying the theme's importance.
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme, with characters constantly facing danger and betrayal. Jesus is pursued by various factions, including those who want to kill him for blasphemy and those who want to use him for their own political agendas. Judas struggles with the decision to betray Jesus, knowing it will lead to his death. The dialogue is filled with warnings of impending doom and the need for vigilance, such as the repeated references to the destruction of the temple and the coming judgment. The pervasive sense of threat significantly influences the characters' actions and decisions, driving the narrative forward.

title: Batman
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The primary conflict is between Batman and the Joker, which escalates throughout the film. The Joker's actions, such as poisoning beauty products with Smilex and threatening to release gas over Gotham, create explicit threats and escalating tension. Batman's efforts to stop the Joker drive the plot, as seen in his investigation of Axis Chemicals and his confrontation with the Joker at the Gotham City Cathedral. The conflict culminates in a high-stakes confrontation where Batman must stop the Joker from killing innocent people, making conflict the central engine of the story.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's conflicts. The film depicts Batman's violent actions against criminals, as well as the Joker's violent acts. Batman uses physical force to stop criminals, as seen when he confronts the muggers in the alley and later battles the Joker's men. The police also rely on force, with Commissioner Gordon ordering officers to shoot to kill. The Joker uses violence to establish dominance and spread chaos, such as poisoning beauty products and killing rival gang members. The narrative climaxes with a violent confrontation between Batman and the Joker, where physical force is the primary means of resolution.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: The police are portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when Eckhardt sets up Napier at Axis Chemicals. The mayor is more concerned with appearances than actual safety, insisting on a festival despite the danger. The commissioner seems powerless to stop corruption within his own department.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a central theme in "Batman" (1989). The film depicts a city rife with corruption, where organized crime, led by Boss Carl Grissom, holds significant sway. This is evident in dialogues where characters like Eckhardt discuss their positions within the criminal hierarchy and their relationship to Grissom. The emergence of Batman introduces a new power dynamic, challenging the established order and creating fear among criminals, as seen in their conversations about the 'bat' and his invincibility. The struggle for control is further emphasized through the actions of Harvey Dent, the district attorney, who vows to dismantle the syndicate, and the Joker, who seeks to usurp Grissom's power and plunge the city into chaos.
extreme_individualism_evidence: The film presents a clear tension between individual action and collective effort, particularly through the character of Batman. He operates outside the law, rejecting the police force's methods, as seen when he tells the muggers to "Tell all your friends about me. I'm Batman." This highlights his self-reliant approach to crime-fighting. The dialogue also frames the police and public officials as "helpless," further emphasizing the need for an individual to take charge. While Harvey Dent aims to make the city safe "together," Batman's actions are largely solitary, and he ultimately resolves the Joker crisis on his own, reinforcing the theme of individual capability.
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The dialogue frequently highlights the dangers of Gotham City, with characters expressing fear of crime and violence. For example, the mayor states, "They won't be scared when you get Grissom in that courthouse," indicating the pervasive fear Grissom instills. The emergence of Batman is directly linked to the city's overwhelming crime, as the police commissioner notes, "Our streets are overrun. Our public officials are helpless." The Joker's actions, such as poisoning beauty products with Smilex, further amplify the sense of vulnerability and environmental threat, leading to widespread panic and a "shopping nightmare."

title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a dominant force in the narrative. The film centers on the pursuit of the Holy Grail, immediately establishing antagonism between Indiana Jones and various adversaries, primarily Nazis, who also seek the artifact. This pursuit involves escalating tension, physical confrontations (e.g., fights, chases), and strategic maneuvering, as characters actively try to outwit and overcome each other. The high stakes are evident in the threats to Jones's life and the potential for the Grail to fall into the wrong hands, shaping character decisions and driving the plot forward. The dialogue explicitly highlights the race against evil and the dangers of the Grail being captured by the Nazis, solidifying conflict as the central engine of the story.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. The narrative repeatedly uses physical confrontation and threats of violence as primary drivers of plot and character action. Indiana Jones frequently resorts to fighting, chasing, and threatening enemies to retrieve artifacts or protect his father. The Brotherhood of the Cruciform Sword actively tries to kill Jones to protect the Grail's secret, and the Nazis use violence and intimidation to pursue their goals. The film's climax involves navigating deadly traps and ultimately choosing the correct Grail to save Jones's father's life, highlighting survival and success through physical and mental challenges under threat of death.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts law enforcement as easily manipulated by powerful individuals, as seen when the sheriff dismisses Indiana's claims about the looted cross and sides with the looters because they have 'witnesses'. Walter Donovan's manipulation of the museum and his betrayal of Indiana Jones further highlight the untrustworthiness of established institutions. The Brotherhood of the Cruciform Sword operates outside the law to protect the Grail, suggesting that formal institutions are inadequate for safeguarding important artifacts. The Nazis' infiltration and exploitation of various organizations, including museums and archaeological projects, underscore the corruption and ineffectiveness of institutions in the face of powerful, malevolent forces.
power_dynamics_evidence: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Donovan directs Jones to find his father and the Grail, Kazim's men attempt to kill Jones to protect the Grail's secret, and the Nazis exert authority over others, such as when they demand the Grail diary and command troops.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Indiana Jones often acts independently, even when others are involved. He states, "I'm going to continue to do things the way I think they should be done," showing a preference for his own methods over collaboration.
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme in "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade." Characters face constant danger from Nazis and other adversaries, driving their actions and decisions. Dialogue such as "Don't trust anybody" and "Be very careful" emphasizes the need for vigilance. The Brotherhood of the Cruciform Sword's willingness to "do anything to keep it safe" highlights the pervasive danger. The narrative is filled with perilous situations, including chases, fights, and booby traps, reinforcing the sense of a dangerous world.

title: Lethal Weapon 2
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles depict a sustained and escalating conflict between the protagonists (Riggs and Murtaugh) and a criminal organization involved in drug trafficking and money laundering. This conflict is established early with high-speed chases and shootouts, and it intensifies as the criminals target the officers and their families. The narrative is driven by the officers' attempts to thwart the criminals' operations, protect a key witness, and avenge the deaths of colleagues and loved ones. The dialogue is replete with threats, confrontations, and escalating stakes, making conflict the central element that shapes the plot and character decisions.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force/violence is a central theme in this film, with numerous instances of its application as a primary means of resolving conflict. The film opens with a high-speed car chase involving gunfire, immediately establishing violence as a key element. Dialogue such as "If you see anybody running out, just pump the shit out of them" and the frequent use of firearms by both the police and criminals highlight the reliance on force. The narrative escalates with threats against the officers' families, leading to retaliatory violence. The climax involves a large-scale shootout on a cargo ship, where the protagonists use lethal force to eliminate the antagonists, underscoring the film's dependence on violence to resolve its central conflicts.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts law enforcement as largely ineffective and easily manipulated by diplomatic immunity, as seen when Rudd and his associates are released despite clear evidence of criminal activity. The dialogue highlights the limitations and frustrations of the police force, with Murtaugh and Riggs often circumventing official channels to pursue justice. The system's inability to hold Rudd accountable forces Riggs to take matters into his own hands, culminating in a violent confrontation where he disregards protocol to achieve justice. The film also portrays corruption within the police force itself, as evidenced by the deaths of Wyler, Collins, and Cavanaugh, who were likely killed for getting too close to the truth.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a central, recurring theme. The film depicts a clear hierarchy within the police force, with characters giving and receiving orders (e.g., "Somebody back off," "Get your slow ass in here!"). There's a constant struggle for dominance, particularly between Riggs and Murtaugh, as they jockey for control in various situations (e.g., "Only if I drive," "Move over. I'll drive."). The South African diplomats assert their authority through diplomatic immunity, highlighting a power imbalance that frustrates the police. The film also shows the abuse of power by the villains, who use violence and intimidation to maintain control over their criminal enterprise (e.g., "After this, it gets bloody," "Tell your people to back off.").
extreme_individualism_evidence: The film features a protagonist, Riggs, who is portrayed as a "lone wolf" type, often disregarding teamwork and authority. Dialogue such as "Sometimes I go nuts" and his general disregard for rules suggest a strong individualistic streak. While he does eventually form a partnership with Murtaugh, the initial tension and Riggs's independent actions contribute to the narrative's conflict. The film also presents instances where collective efforts, such as police procedures, are circumvented by Riggs's individual actions, further emphasizing the theme.
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The dialogue frequently emphasizes danger, vulnerability, and the need for vigilance. The film opens with a high-speed chase and shootout, immediately establishing a dangerous environment. Characters are constantly at risk of harm, as evidenced by the threats against Murtaugh's family ("Wondering about your kids? About what we've done to them?") and the targeting of police officers ("We lost Wyler, Collins, Cavanaugh. How many do we have to lose?"). Riggs's backstory of loss and his willingness to engage in dangerous behavior further reinforces the theme of pervasive threat.

title: Honey, I Shrunk the Kids
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film establishes conflict early with the bickering neighbors, the Szalinskis and Thompsons, and their sons' rivalry. Wayne Szalinski's scientific ambition clashes with professional skepticism, creating external pressure. The core conflict arises when the children are accidentally shrunk, forcing them to navigate a dangerous backyard and survive threats like insects and lawnmowers. This external threat escalates tension and shapes the children's decisions, as well as the parents' frantic search and eventual reconciliation, making conflict a dominant force in the plot.
force_as_resolution_evidence: Force/violence is present but not dominant. There are instances of aggression, such as Ron's violent tendencies and the father's desire for his son to be physically stronger. Ron hits a baseball through the neighbor's window, and later threatens his brother with physical harm. The father, Russ, also makes aggressive comments about breaking the neighbor's arm. However, these instances are balanced by other problem-solving methods, such as communication and teamwork, especially when the children are shrunk. The narrative does not solely rely on force to resolve conflicts, but it is a recurring element.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. Wayne Szalinski faces skepticism and ridicule from his peers at the conference regarding his shrinking machine, suggesting a lack of open-mindedness within the scientific community. He is dismissed as "hardly Einstein" and his work is not taken seriously without immediate proof. Additionally, when the parents report their children missing, the police officer seems dismissive and unconcerned, implying a lack of diligence or empathy from law enforcement. However, these instances do not form the core of the narrative, which focuses more on family dynamics and survival.
power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a recurring theme, primarily within the family relationships. The father, Wayne, struggles to assert authority over his children, particularly Russell, pushing him to participate in activities like fishing and football despite Russell's lack of interest. This is evident in lines like, "And you're coming fishing with the family. Is that clear? I can't hear you! Yes, sir." Similarly, Russ Thompson's father, Don, displays a need to dominate and control situations, evident in his interactions with his wife and his insistence on going on the fishing trip. The children also engage in power struggles, such as Ron's bullying behavior towards Nick and the negotiation over mowing the lawn.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Individualism is present but not dominant. Wayne Szalinski is portrayed as a somewhat eccentric inventor who often prioritizes his work over family needs, leading to some friction. For example, his wife Diane says, "I failed, Diane. I-I... I'm just gonna get my old job back, if I can get my old job back. But from now on, things are gonna be different." This suggests a pattern of behavior where his individual pursuits have negatively impacted his family life. However, the narrative also emphasizes the importance of family unity and cooperation, especially when the children are shrunk. The resolution depends on the family working together, suggesting that teamwork is ultimately valued.
perceived_threat_evidence: The film presents a world where everyday environments pose significant dangers, particularly after the children are shrunk. Dialogue emphasizes vulnerability, such as Amy's fear of pollen ("It's too big! I'm too little to breathe it in!") and Nick's warning about the cat ("It's that stupid cat of theirs!"). The children face threats from insects, lawnmowers, and even the well-intentioned actions of their parents, highlighting a constant need for vigilance. The narrative relies on the children's struggle to survive in a familiar yet hostile environment, making perceived threat a recurring theme.

title: Look Who's Talking
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is a central element in this film. Mollie faces recurring antagonism from Albert's wife and the social stigma of being a single mother. The narrative is driven by the escalating tension between Mollie's desire for a stable family and the complications arising from her relationships, particularly Albert's inability to commit and James's initial reluctance to embrace fatherhood. force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are present, but not central to resolving the narrative's core conflicts. institutional_cynicism_evidence: The dialogue shows a distrust of doctors and hospitals, with the mother in labor demanding drugs and questioning the medical staff's competence. The cab driver's constant scams and illegal activities, like using someone else's address for residency and getting free lunches, highlight a disregard for rules and laws. title: License to Kill
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict between James Bond and drug lord Sanchez. Bond's subsequent pursuit of Sanchez drives the plot, leading to numerous confrontations, betrayals, and escalating stakes, as seen in the dialogue: "Effective immediately, your licence to kill is revoked." and "I won't be safe until Sanchez is dead."

Characters like Dario are introduced as violent enforcers, and Bond himself resorts to aggressive tactics, including killing multiple individuals, to disrupt Sanchez's operations. The climax involves a violent confrontation where Bond uses explosives and physical force to destroy Sanchez's drug operation and ultimately kill Sanchez himself, demonstrating that force is the primary means of achieving justice and resolving the conflict.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. This prompts Bond's resignation and rogue pursuit of Sanchez. The dialogue highlights the systemic corruption that allows Sanchez to operate with impunity, as Leiter explains, "He's killed, intimidated or bribed half the officials from here to Chile. power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are central to the narrative, primarily revolving around the drug lord Sanchez and his control over his organization and various authorities. Dialogue frequently highlights Sanchez's dominance, such as when he states, "Loyalty is more important to me than money," showcasing his demand for absolute obedience. The film also depicts the enforcement of hierarchies through violence and intimidation, as seen in the treatment of those who betray or displease Sanchez. Furthermore, the constant struggle for leverage and control is evident in interactions between characters, such as Bond's infiltration of Sanchez's organization and his attempts to subvert the established power structure, as well as the power plays between Sanchez and corrupt officials like President Lopez.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Bond operates largely outside of official channels, driven by personal vengeance after Leiter is attacked. He resigns from MI6 when his superiors order him to drop the case, declaring, "I owe it to Leiter." This sets him on a path of independent action, rejecting the authority and resources of his organization. Although he receives some assistance from Q, Bond consistently asserts his need to work alone, telling Q, "I work better alone." and Pam, "Enough people are dead."
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, with characters frequently expressing fear and vulnerability. The dialogue emphasizes the dangerous nature of Sanchez and his operations, creating a pervasive sense of unease. Characters are constantly at risk of betrayal, violence, and death, as evidenced by lines like, "You're facin' 139 felony counts, Sanchez. The narrative is driven by Bond's pursuit of Sanchez, fueled by the brutal attack on Leiter and the constant threat Sanchez poses to those around him. The world is portrayed as a dangerous place where trust is scarce, and even allies can turn against each other, as seen with Killifer's betrayal: "Sorry, old buddy, but two mill is a hell of a chunk of dough."

title: Fletch Lives

The narrative also includes the violent actions of the KKK and the eventual shootout at the climax, further emphasizing the role of force in resolving conflicts.
institutional_cynicism_evidence: The film presents a world where institutions are frequently flawed, corrupt, or ineffective, driving significant plot points. power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a recurring theme, though not the central engine of the narrative. Fletch frequently encounters individuals attempting to exert control or manipulate him. While these struggles are significant, the narrative also focuses on Fletch's investigation and personal relationships, preventing power dynamics from becoming the sole focus.
extreme_individualism_evidence: Individualism is present but not dominant. The protagonist, Fletch, often operates independently, using disguises and wit to navigate situations, as seen when he investigates the Greek seafood house and later when he infiltrates the Bly Bio Chem plant. He frequently disregards authority and established procedures, such as when he manipulates situations to his advantage, like his interactions with the police and his handling of his alimony situation with Gillet. However, he also relies on information and assistance from others, such as Frank at the newspaper and Calculus, indicating a degree of cooperation. The narrative doesn't consistently frame collective efforts as weak, and Fletch's actions, while often individualistic, ultimately serve a broader purpose of uncovering corruption, suggesting a balance between individual initiative and community well-being.
perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. Fletch encounters danger in various forms, including attempts on his life. For example, he says, "Three guys tried to kill me," indicating a direct threat to his safety. The dialogue also reveals a sense of paranoia and distrust, as characters are often suspicious of each other's motives. The sheriff's initial hostility and the KKK's intimidation tactics contribute to an atmosphere of danger and the need for vigilance. title: Dangerous Liaisons
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film. force_as_resolution_evidence: Force and violence are moderately central to the narrative's resolution. institutional_cynicism_evidence: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are central to the narrative, with characters constantly maneuvering for social and interpersonal dominance. The dialogue is replete with examples of characters attempting to control or manipulate others. Madame de Merteuil explicitly states her intention to "dominate your sex and avenge my own," and much of her dialogue revolves around strategies for achieving this. Valmont's pursuit of Madame de Tourvel is framed as a conquest, a challenge to his reputation, and a means of asserting his power. The relationships between characters, such as Merteuil and Valmont, are often transactional, with each seeking to gain leverage over the other. Even seemingly innocuous interactions, like those between Cecile and others, are often tinged with manipulation and control.
extreme_individualism_evidence: The film explores the tension between individual desires and societal expectations, particularly through the characters of Valmont and Merteuil. Their pursuit of personal pleasure and revenge often disregards the well-being of others. Valmont's initial reluctance to seduce Madame de Tourvel because "it's too easy" and his later desire to "betray everything that's most important to her" highlights a focus on individual conquest over collective morality. Merteuil's manipulation of others to avenge her sex and dominate men further emphasizes this individualism. While the narrative does not entirely dismiss the importance of social connections, the characters' actions are primarily driven by self-interest and a desire for personal triumph, making the tension between individual ambition and collective well-being a recurring theme.
perceived_threat_evidence: A recurring sense of threat and vulnerability is present, though not dominant. Characters are often wary of each other's intentions, and reputation is a fragile thing that can be ruined by "a few well-chosen words." Valmont's actions, such as manipulating the poor family and his pursuit of Madame de Tourvel, suggest a predatory environment. The dialogue hints at a constant need for vigilance and awareness of potential betrayal, contributing to a moderate sense of perceived threat.

title: Weekend at Bernie's

power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are a recurring theme, primarily revolving around workplace hierarchy and the assertion of dominance. title: Lean on Me
structural_conflict_evidence: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. institutional_cynicism_evidence: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. power_dynamics_evidence: Power dynamics are central to the narrative, primarily revolving around Joe Clark's methods as principal. perceived_threat_evidence: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative.
